Many successful campaigns for social awareness or promoting social causes are rapidly circulated on these platforms, and talked about across thousands of repost trees. A microblog repost tree is a directed graph rooted at the original message (leader, also called the seed instance), and includes messages that directly or indirectly repost and reference the original message and each other. Analyzing microblog repost trees has the potential to uncover useful and timely insights into social phenomena and aggregate people's perception (e.g., for tracking public opinions during election campaigns (Chen et al., 2013;Gilbert and Karahalios, 2009)). We propose a novel repost tree summarization framework by effectively differentiating two kinds of messages in repost trees called leaders and followers, which are derived from two fundamental content-level structure information: (1) the contents of messages and (2) the reposting relations between the messages, which together make up a repost tree. However, their adaptation relied heavily on language resources (annotated corpus for query paths, etc.) which are available in most web search engines and corporate search systems but difficult to obtain outside this context. Our work explores a different path to develop a neural model for parsing web queries which can handle their unique structure without requiring the training corpus resources. To address this, we need a model that can handle training on monolingual data without explicit language identification and yet output part-of-speech (POS) tags for code-switched text. This paper proposes a novel model architecture that can jointly maintain separate word representations for each of the language of interest, as well as any possible script in case of transliteration. The model is trained on monolingual data and can be applied to unseen mixed-language texts at inference time, without any explicit language identification. The model can thus profit from training data that is prevalent and easier to collect, while fitting in naturally with code-switched scenarios where line-by-line language identification may be difficult or even impossible without comprehensive contextual knowledge. The key idea of our approach is to use separate embedding components for each language of interest, so that each language has its own representation, yet the paths through these components can be combined in the framework of Transformer-based models, which we use for hierarchical modeling. Figure 1 illustrates the model structure. Each word representation or sub-representation is embedded in a separate embedding component which can be thought of as a 'language-or-script' identifier. These components are expected to interact during sequential prediction by means of the Transformer's self-attention mechanism. In this way, the model can learn associations between the sub-representations and the target POS tag, while retaining the distinctness of the language or script from which each sub-representation was derived. An important point worth mentioning is that the model can handle cases where a text switches languages multiple times. In practice, our methodology opens a door to developing models that can operate effectively across monolingual and code-switching scenarios using a consistent underlying architecture. Image retrieval tasks, where the goal is to rank a collection of images using a user-supplied query, have many practical applications in organization, analysis and search for multimedia data. In spite of this, research efforts in image retrieval face questions such as "What is the right level and granularity of representation for an image?" and "How can a representation incorporate spatial and semantic relationships within an image?" Currently, many state-of-the-art image retrieval methods represent each image as a bag-of-features, which is indeed a simple representation but not without limitations (Fergus et al, 2010). A bag-of-features representation treats each image independently, considering features such as SIFT (Lowe, 1999) or semantic features (Xiao et al, 2010) as a collection of independent features. While this type of representation is effective for retrieving exact matches or images containing specific object configurations (e.g., a query image of a yellow flower might match images with the same color and similar shape), it falls short in handling more complex scenarios, for example, where the retrieval goal is related to interactions or dependencies between different objects within an image. The limitation of bag-of-features representations becomes particularly apparent when trying to understand the relationship between multiple objects within an image. For example, in an image of a scene in a kitchen, a retrieval system might return images of kitchen scenes, but it might not correctly distinguish between scenes with people using kitchen utensils and those without. This is because the bag-of-features representation does not provide any information about how the objects in an image interact or relate to each other, beyond their co-occurrence. To address this limitation, we propose the use of Visual Dependency Representations (VDRs). VDRs are designed to model the spatial and semantic dependencies between objects and regions within an image (Figure 1). By encoding these dependencies, VDRs can capture more nuances in image content and thus, potentially, perform better in retrieval tasks where dependencies between objects matter, such as when querying for "images of people interacting with objects." This paper presents an approach to image retrieval that uses VDRs for the representation of both images and queries. Our proposed system allows a user to query for images by providing an example image. The system then finds images that are most similar to the given example based on the VDR representations. The goal is to assign an appropriate discourse relation label between each pair of consecutive sentences in a text. The challenge of discourse parsing lies in the inherently hierarchical nature of text where structural relationships can span across multiple sentences, and where ambiguity and noise (e.g., typos, incorrect punctuation) are common due to the complexity of human language. Recent advances in deep learning, particularly with the introduction of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and more recently, attention mechanisms, have provided powerful tools for sequence labeling tasks like discourse parsing. However, while semantic features (i.e., the content of sentences or words) are crucial for making sense of discourse relationships, traditional sequence labeling approaches often fail to fully leverage such semantic information due to being mainly focused on surface-level features like word identity and surrounding context. This work addresses these limitations by proposing a discourse parsing model that combines the strengths of hierarchical neural networks with attention mechanisms. This approach allows for a more nuanced understanding of the discourse structure by considering both the sequential dependencies between sentences and the latent semantic features that might influence the relationship between them. We specifically explore an architecture that can capture both local (sentence-level) and global (sentence pair-level) features, enabling the model to reason about more complex forms of discourse structure. The contribution of this work is twofold: 1. **Hierarchical Architecture**: We introduce a hierarchical neural network model for discourse parsing that can capture both the sequential and the structural complexities of discourse. response: Autoregressive (AR) models are widely used in sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) tasks such as machine translation. In an AR model, the encoder and decoder are normally assumed to be single RNNs. The main downside of these AR models is their slow decoding speed due to the sequential and left-to-right nature of the recurrent units in the decoder. Decoding one word at each step leads to decoding times proportional to the target length. This makes them ill-suited for generating long sentences and large language models. In practice, decoder branches are split to decode multiple words in parallel for speed up during testing, even though training still remains slow. However, these simple parallelizing schemes do not optimize the inference speed optimization in the model design phase. To address the problem of slow decoding speed, we propose a new model that keeps the autoregressive property in global but relieves the constraint in local. We call this model semi-autoregressive Transformer (SAT). The SAT implements the AR property globally while producing multiple words in parallel, known as being semi-autoregressive. The SAT also reduces the complexity of inference, leading to a considerable speedup during decoding. In particular, in this paper, we will mainly focus on applying the proposed SAT model to Neural Machine Translation (NMT) tasks. NMT has become the state-of-the-art approach for translation between many different language pairs (Sutskever et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2016). However, as mentioned before, existing AR model-based NMT techniques can have high decoding costs due to their sequential generation process. The MT task is also especially well-suited for summarization of the proposed SAT model, since the correct translation typically preserves the sequential order of the words and the contexts they generate. The SAT model design introduces two key changes from previous AR NMT models. First, instead of a single recurrent unit to generate the next word, the proposed SAT uses multiple recurrent units or parallel attention heads in the decoder. This allows multiple words to be generated together in parallel. However, the order of the predicted words are still controlled by AR relations. Another key change is the use of a global information summary to guide the parallelly and semi-autoregressively generated words. This summary is usually shared by all parallelly generated words. This helps to ensure that all generated words make sense when viewed together, not in isolation. The summary is either a set of contextual features, past decoder states, or an aggregation of all previously generated words. The first of such proposals are the show, attend and tell model (Ba et al., 2016). This model allows the decoder to recover from mistakes made in previous time steps by attending to previous decoded states plus the current encoder states. We propose an extension of this idea. However, the idea of using global summaries to guide parallel word generation is taken one-step further in this work. The global information is updated and any word generation errors are corrected at a global auto-regressive step. This correction step is separate from the parallel generation step, and runs forward through the sequence, from right to left (or some other order), just like the standard autoregressive model. This dual process allows the proposed SAT model to enjoy both the predictive benefits of successful global summary functions and the speed-up gain of parallel word generation. We found that the trade-off between fast parallel generation and global coherence correction is manageable and allows for good balance between performance and speed. Another key innovation is to realize that for translation, having a partial and meaningful translation is often better than waiting for a slower model, especially when the cost of waiting is high

While natural language understanding tasks have seen significant advances, understanding of various constructs, including conditional statements (e.g., "if A then B"), remains challenging, particularly because these statements do not have a simple syntactic or semantic pattern (Asher and Smith, 2011). A "rule" in this context may take the form of an if-then statement, such as "If it is going to rain tomorrow, then carry an umbrella." Understanding if-then statements is not limited to digital personal assistants; it is also a central aspect of clinical decision support systems (Shortliffe, 1987), business rules engines (Vanthienen, 2011), among others. Such systems can be used to encode clinical guidelines (e.g., "If the patient has fever AND a positive lung X-ray THEN prescribe antibiotics"), business processes (e.g., "If the sale is over $100 AND the customer has been a premium member for at least 6 months THEN apply a 10% discount"), or even user-defined "if-then" rules in general-purpose programming tools. Semantic parsing (Zelle and Mooney, 1996; Wong and Mooney, 2006; Kwiatkowski et al., 2013) – translating natural language to a formal, executable representation – is a core component of such systems. Despite progress over the years (Collier et al., 2007; Liang et al., 2016), state-of-the-art semantic parsers, even those that handle if-then constructs, still face limitations in accuracy, robustness, and scalability. This paper focuses on the challenge of improved semantic parsing specifically for if-then statements. Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), proposed by Blei et al. (2003), is one such powerful NLP technique used for topic modeling and document clustering. At its core, LDA is a generative probabilistic model that can capture the underlying structure of a collection of documents and thereby identify key topics. The model assumes that each document is composed of a mixture of topics, and each topic is a distribution over word types, which helps in identifying recurring themes or subjects within the corpus. However, despite its efficacy, LDA, like many other topic modeling techniques, is not entirely without its limitations. One of the chief issues in the LDA framework is the pre-processing step required to handle frequently occurring words, often referred to as 'stopwords'. As Blei et al. (2003) and many subsequent studies have noted, high-frequency words such as 'the', 'and', 'a', etc., which may not provide much semantic value, tend to dominate many or even all the topics in the model. The uniform treatment of all words in LDA, without any attempt to quantify their contribution to the topics, has led practitioners to often resort to the elimination of these stopwords before the application of LDA. This pre-processing step is not only somewhat arbitrary, but also neglects potential insights that high-frequency words might offer, especially when used in specific contexts. While term weighting techniques, akin to those used in Latent Semantic Indexing (LSI), could address this issue, they have not been systematically explored in the context of LDA. Unlike LSI, where term weights are often derived from the tf-idf (term frequency-inverse document frequency) scheme, LDA focuses on the probabilistic distribution of words across topics without the explicit notion of term weighting. More specifically, in LDA, the probability of a word belonging to a topic is determined by the word's distribution over topics, and this distribution is learned from data without explicit term weights. The lack of term weighting in LDA can lead to several problems. Firstly, it may disproportionately emphasize high-frequency words, leading to a condition often called "topic dilution" (Blei et al., 2003). Here, certain words, because of their high occurrence across the corpus, may be overrepresented across multiple topics, potentially masking the existence of other, distinct topics. Secondly, without term weighting, it becomes difficult to discern which words truly belong to a topic and which are just statistical artifacts, particularly when dealing with a large vocabulary and a relatively small corpus. This paper proposes a novel approach to incorporate term weighting into the LDA framework. We argue that by using a well-suited term weighting scheme, it is possible to improve the interpretability and utility of topics extracted by LDA, especially in applications where understanding the semantic role of specific words within their respective topics is critical (e.g., in information retrieval, text classification, and semantic analysis). Firstly, we extend the LDA model to allow for term weights, enabling a more nuanced understanding of word importance within topics. Bilingual term alignment aims to map terms (or words) in two languages to each other. In the last few years, Sequence-to-Sequence (Seq2seq) deep learning models (Sutskever et al., 2014) have been successfully applied to the task, and many variations have been proposed to improve performance (Nallapati et al., 2016; See et al., 2017; Tolstikhin et al., 2017; Gu et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2018). Despite these advances, the generated summaries still often retain essential word omissions or inaccuracies in the retrieved key phrases, leading to a decreased informativeness of the output. These omissions are likely due to the lack of a proper treatment of the semantic structure of the source text in the proposed models. In earlier work (Liu et al., 2018), we established that certain information, such as the dependency structure of source sentences, serves as a strong cue for automatic summarization. We introduced a structured copy mechanism that can automatically generate coherent summaries from hierarchical text representations. However, previous structure-infused copy mechanisms suffer from a major limitation: they rely on manually specified patterns which can prevent the models from fully exploring the hidden syntax of the source text. 2 To overcome this challenge, we propose in this paper a novel structured copy mechanism that infers the syntactic dependency structure of the source sentence to guide sentence generation. In constructing various forms of lexical networks, including co-occurrence networks, author-topic networks, and semantic networks, a common practice is to use some kind of semantic orientation to represent the strength or polarity of semantic relationships among the nodes (e.g., words or terms) in the network. For instance, in the co-occurrence network, word-pairs presenting strong positive correlation (e.g., "sunny day") and negative correlation (e.g., "rainy day") are frequently used to build a polarity lexicon – a dictionary where words are associated with sentiment scores. Statistical mechanical methods have been increasingly popular in understanding the properties and behaviors of such lexical networks among semantic orientations. One of the most notable examples is the Ising spin model adopted in the context of sentiment analysis (Gomez-Rodriguez et al., 2008; Baccianella et al., 2010; Droghini et al., 2015). The general idea behind using the Ising model is to represent the semantic or sentiment orientations (polarities) of words as uniform spins, which are identified as +1 or -1 for positive and negative sentiment respectively. The interaction strength between word-pairs is quantified by the weight matrix based on the observed co-occurrence frequency or its variants. The model is then used to infer the semantic orientations of words or documents by using techniques from statistical mechanics, such as maximizing the entropy of the system under certain constraints. A key feature of the Ising model as applied to sentiment analysis is the reported presence of phase transitions in the vicinity of the optimal "temperature" parameter (Baccianella et al., 2010; Droghini et al., 2015). Similar phase transitions have also been observed in other probabilistic models such as the Boltzmann machine used in topic modeling (Hinton, 2012). The idea of a phase transition in NLP is intriguing: it suggests that there is a critical point around which the system's behaviors suddenly change and the model’s performance peaks. response: Recognising Entailment within Discourse Introduction Inferential language processing's most studied problem is textual entailment (TE). Two TE systems are given a pair of text snippets, e.g., the original and a paraphrase, and need to decide whether one entails the other (entailment), contradicts it (contradiction), or if this relation is unknown (neutral). The TE problem has various applications such as question answering, idiom understanding, textual entailment detectors (Chopra, 2015), among others. Recognising entailment requires understanding both the context and meaning of the texts, something that most TE systems have primarily focused on meaning, disregarding textual context (extraction based on the text itself) and verbal context (extraction based on features such as similarity of words, word correlations, etc..) (Bosch et al., 2005), and recent systems also ignore discourse context. A comprehensive study on the importance of discourse context in TE is still lacking, but its significance arises from several reasons. Firstly, discourse context can clarify otherwise ambiguous sentences. Suppose a sentence S is similar to a sentence P and S entails P. However, between them there is a sentence R which orients interpretation towards the negative For instance, R could be a sentence that describes S as 'Surprisingly S' or 'R is the expected answer, but S is true', in the latter case S should actually be taken in opposition to P. Furthermore, discourse structure, coreference, anaphora, and presupposition, among other aspects (Prince, 1981) play a significant role, especially in complex reasoning akin to text-based reasoning or more formal contexts. One could argue that the TE problem captures a part of this problem and that a better treatment of discourse could likely improve TE models in complex scenarios where the context plays a more significant role. For example, 'The delivery of the package to the wrong apartment was caused by the lack of the correct address. This was true for the whole block.' Here a discourse level observation (the package being for the whole block) is required to understand the relation between the couple of sentences and determine entailment. Domain adaptation is a well-studied problem that seeks to develop methods to handle the drastically different distributions of text, semantics, and language across domains. A common situation is one where labeled training data is available in one domain (say the source domain), but the task at hand requires the inference and prediction to occur in another domain (the target domain). Bootstrapping is a semi-supervised methodology that keeps improving model performance on a task by adding randomly sampled examples that the model itself classifies, along with their labels. However, when dealing with domain adaptation problems, simply adding examples to the training set from a different domain may degrade performance, as these examples may carry domain-specific features that are not present in the target domain or even introduce bias. In this paper, we address the problem of domain adaptive bootstrapping for named entity recognition (NER) where standard bootstrapping techniques are known to suffer. We propose a framework that adaptively selects unlabeled examples from the target domain (which we term "bridges") that carry features which both the model is likely to get right and that are semantically common to both the source and target domains. Our approach seeks to strike a balance between the bias introduced by the source domain, while still leveraging the available label data in the source domain. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our technique by conducting thorough experiments on several carefully selected named entity recognition datasets that span diverse domains. Our results show that our domain adaptive bootstrapping approach consistently outperforms in-domain training, standard bootstrapping, transductive learning, and a few baseline domain adaptation methods. The impact of this work doesn't dwell only in the specific task of named entity recognition; the principle of domain adaptive bootstrapping can be extended to other NLP tasks or structured prediction problems where the source and target domains exhibit different distributions, and where exploiting both labeled and unlabeled data from the target domain is advantageous. Several NLP tasks benefit from domain adaptation, but few integrate bootstrapping as part of their adaptation strategies. Our approach is systematic in identifying discriminative and common patterns across domains that are identifiable through the model’s predictions, which then form the backbone for model improvement. The bootstrapping step in this new framework operates not just on random examples but on those selected because they are likely to be added to the training data with greater utility given the domain adaptation goal. response: Training embeddings with composed softmax objective or other structured prediction objectives has become a recent trend in NLP. Many successful applications of these models have involved decomposing meaning and reasoning over its components, implicitly using this structure to inform their predictions. Models that learn to predict compositionally have been applied to tasks as diverse and challenging as entailment detection (Min et al., 2014), paraphrasing and textual similarity (Kembhavi et al., 2017), natural language inference (Cheng and Hockenmaier, 2016) and script learning for commonsense reasoning (Bowman et al., 2015;Bowman et al., 2016). However, unlike many other areas such as visual object detection, where we can directly check alignment of model predictions with hand-labelling, or sequence-to-sequence models, where we can sample from the model directly to assess the range of linguistic outputs that might be generated, we have less direct access to the notion of compositional meaning being captured within a learned embedding. One key reason for this is that the neural models used in these settings are often deeply complex and it is unclear which aspects of the inputs and weights contribute to the compositional or non-compositional aspects of the representation. To develop a more nuanced understanding of how well these models represent compositional meaning in the sense of capturing how linguistic form and assumed world knowledge combine to give sentential meaning, in this paper we develop a series of tasks that allow the extraction of compositional information directly from learned sentence embeddings. 2 By compositional meaning here, we mean meaning that is represented in terms of parts or components of sentences and in terms of the way these components interact syntactically and semantically. We focus on embedding models and their ability to represent compositional information: how well can they capture that it is the interaction and the structure that determines meaning? The tasks we propose aim to highlight understanding on all levels of compositional analysis, from the sub-lexical to the syntactic, and together they help to address the gap between the static vector space of the embedding and our intuitive notions of meaning as composition of explicitly structured parts. By comparing how readily a set of generated sentences, each meeting specific formal constraints, can be represented within the embedding space of the given model 3, the tasks we introduce allow for the extraction of structured information about the capacity of embedding models to represent linguistic composition. WSD deals with the problem of determining the intended meaning or sense of a particular word, typically a noun, in context. NEL, on the other hand, is concerned with linking mentions of named entities (i.e., real-world objects like people, places, and organizations) to their corresponding entries in a knowledge base, thereby providing grounding and further information for these entities extracted from text. These tasks are closely related in many NLP applications. For example, word senses and named entities often co-occur in text, and disambiguating a word's sense can inform the NEL process. Conversely, having linked named entities can help disambiguate words that refer to these entities. Jointly addressing WSD and NEL can thus reduce ambiguity and provide richer and more accurate NLP results. However, the joint problem of disambiguating nouns and linking named entities remains challenging. Traditional approaches might treat these tasks separately, even though they share many potential useful features and inference constraints. For example, referential context (such as pronouns, verb arguments) that aids in NEL can also inform WSD, while semantic similarity among word senses can predict potential candidates for NEL. Another challenge is the multi-faceted nature of the disambiguation problem. A word might have multiple senses, some of which are more relevant in certain contexts. Meanwhile, entities can have various forms or aliases, and each mention could refer to the same, a different, or even multiple entities (e.g., ambiguity between people sharing the same name). Source code isn't written in a vacuum. It is deeply intertwined with the programmatic environment in which it operates, primarily the class or structure that it is a part of. This interdependence means that the appropriate form and content of code are very much context-dependent. A clear understanding of this interplay is critical for both programming education and the development of tools that can assist developers in various ways—from code completion to automatic documentation. Yet, the nature of how language is mapped to code within a programmatic context has received relatively little attention. The task of mapping language to appropriate code in the context of programming marks a significant frontier in the applications of NLP to software development and understanding. This paper introduces the task of generating class member functions given English documentation and the programmatic context provided by the rest of the class. This is distinct from existing NLP tasks related to code generation because it explicitly requires accounting for the class environment. For instance, in a class that implements a data structure like a stack, the documentation for a method such as "get first element" must rely on existing implementations within the class (if any) to determine how, exactly, this is achieved. However, real-world texts often contain multiple events intertwined, making the extraction of multiple events more challenging than handling a single event (Chieu and Ng, 2002;Nguyen and Lapata, 2015). Traditionally, approaches to event extraction have focused primarily on modeling events in isolation, using sequential models such as recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks. These models process text sequentially, making them well-suited for capturing local dependencies but limited in their ability to handle long-range dependencies between multiple events within the same sentence. Hence, while these models can effectively extract single events, they are less effective at identifying and relating multiple events within a sentence due to their sequential nature, which can lead to information loss across events. In this paper, we tackle the problem of Jointly Multiple Events Extraction (JMEE) by introducing a novel framework that explicitly addresses the challenges of extracting multiple events within a single sentence. Our framework is based on the idea of aggregating information across multiple events using both syntactic and semantic graph structures in a more efficient and effective manner than purely sequential approaches. We hypothesize that enhancing information flow between events and using graph-based models for aggregating information can significantly improve the task of jointly extracting multiple events, especially in complex scenarios where events are deeply intertwined. response: Certainly, here is my answer: Introduction Multi-label learning (Zhou et al., 2004; Torresani et al., 2010) is a type of structured prediction problem, where a set of labels can be assigned to each instance. Many real-world applications are inherently multi-label, such as product categorization on Amazon or topic modeling in large-scale document corpora (Ehret and Ngai, 2016;Stratos and Nie, 2015). In text classification, there are typically thousands (or tens of thousands) of possible labels (for instance, Wikipedia's category system contains over 100K categories), and an instance may belong to multiple labels (coughing is both a symptom and a disease, for instance). Even in a large training dataset, we cannot cover all possible labels. This is especially true for large-scale classification problems, such as the medical domain (MIMIC, Bian et al., 2020;Chatbot, Chen et al., 2019), where labels are highly specific and user-defined. Recent advances have introduced methods that can handle these problems, such as Hierarchical Label Space Multi-label Learning (HLML, Rios et al., 2020), which incorporates domain knowledge on the label space. However, these methods typically assume either training data for all possible labels or a strong prior assumed on the label assignments beyond the classification label. This sets up the research question for this paper: Can we develop methods that effectively handle the multi-label prediction problem when there is little (few-shot), or no (zero-shot), training data for a large number of target labels? A key challenge for multi-label few-and zero-shot learning, and a focus of this paper, is that rare labels have very little evidence in the training data (e.g., a few instances for a few-shot label). The issue is compounded for zero-shot labels, which have no instances in training. response: Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) is one of the key challenges in natural language processing. Given a word in context, WSD aims at determining the intended sense of the word, or, failing that, the intended main meaning. WSD has long been recognized as one indispensable step towards the development of more sophisticated NLP applications, such as machine translation, text summarization, and machine reading comprehension. A variety of WSD approaches have been proposed, with most of them relying heavily on large pre-trained lexicons of senses, as well as on appropriate word representations (e.g. word embeddings). For example, (Banerjee and Pedersen, 2002) propose to use WordNet senses to predict word Senses while (Xue et al., 2015) use a combination of WordNet senses, Glove word vectors, and dependency paths. These approaches perform well on high-frequent sense words but are generally considered inadequate on lower-frequent sense words and multi-sense words. As such, the project of identifying all possible senses of a word in context, and thus providing a more complete framework, remains largely unsolved. Recent work has started to tackle the problem of multi-sense Word Sense Disambiguation or All-Words WSD For instance, (Pitler and Nenkova, 2008) predict all senses for each word in the input sentence and then combine the predicted senses using sentential evidence. This approach works reasonably well when the evaluation is conducted at the sentence level, but results at the word level (i.e., for each word in the input sentence) are still inaccurate especially for less frequent senses. Another approach is to predict only the predominant sense of each word based on context, which works well for all contexts but only identifies the "dominant" sense of the word in a given context (e.g. the noun "bank" has different senses as a "financial institution" and as a "water feature or landform"). However the problem of less frequent senses and truly multi-sense words remains a difficult one, as demonstrated recently by (Ng et al., 2015) when they explicitly analyzed the issue and found that while they are able to disambiguate up to 80% of the words in dependency parsers on standard datasets they still can do poorly on 20% of the words. Specifically, they show that for words with high polysemy (meaning that they have many senses), the results of WSD systems remains poor. Recently, there has been a growing interest in the theoretical limits of WSD. For example, (Neviarouskis and McCarthy, 2010) and (Croft, 2010) showed that WSD is an NP-complete problem. This implies that it will be impossible to find a polynomial-time algorithm for WSD that can disambiguate all word senses across all possible contexts for any word in a language. However, the impractical nature of this theoretical result does not deter from the potential of using WSD in NLP tasks, as can be seen in a variety of works using WSD to improve other applications (e.g., (Baroni et al., 2014); (AbuJarour et al., 2015); (Søgaard and Goldberg, 2016)). While the focus of many recent approaches to WSD has been on developing better disambiguation algorithms using deep learning, word embeddings, or dependency parsing, a key issue remains largely unaddressed: the data on which these algorithms are trained and evaluated

response: Certainly, here is my answer: Introduction Machine translation (MT) systems have made significant progress over the past few years, but they still struggle with transliterating proper nouns, or names. These include person, place, and organization names. Names carry important information and indispensable for almost all translation and language processing tasks, but they are often excluded or given minimal treatment in traditional MT approaches (Cohn and Lapata, 2010). The difficulty of handling names arises from several sources. One, of course, is the sheer number of names in the text and the variation in how these names are translated (e.g., different people having the same name, or multiple transliterations for one name). MT systems have traditionally handled names using lists of named entities, often by having a separate NER module in the pipeline. However, this approach is limited, as among other issues, names can be context-dependent (e.g., "Ford" could mean an automobile or a person) and sometimes names are not annotated correctly, which results in incorrect translations being used. Our work proposes a creative yet very intuitive solution - the Name-aware Machine Translation (NameAwareMT) system. This system aims to tackle the name translation problem at the core of the translation process. Our approach utilizes a combination of techniques which tightly integrate name processing within the MT model. First, we propose a novel annotation scheme to label names specifically in parallel corpora while adding this information to the existing parallel data sets. Second, we extract name-aware translation rules and grammars from these annotated corpora, which will guide the MT model to better handle names (especially those that are significantly different across languages). Next, we introduce a dedicated name phrase table for each language pair to capture the specific translation patterns of names. And lastly, we modify the decoder of the MT model to learn from the annotated name data and incorporate "name-driven decoding" which encourages the model to choose name translations that align with the source language's terminology (e.g., using "Microsoft" instead of "微软" for a Chinese-English translation of the company name). We also noticed that traditional MT evaluation metrics might not be sufficient to assess the performance of name translation accurately. Specifically, names and informative words in general should carry a higher value than general words in a translation (for example, in a document about corporations, company names are more important than some general terms). Our solution for this shortfall is a new, importance-weighting translation metric. This metric assigns different weights to different words based on their importance in a document. This ensures that the quality of name translations (or of other significant words) is appropriately assessed and prioritized. We experimented with our Name-awareMT system on translating Chinese to English. The experiments show significant improvements in overall translation quality, especially for name translation and word alignment compared to a well-known MT baseline such as Google Translate or the Moses toolkit when given name-annotated corpus but no specialized name processing. We conclude that the proposed Name-awareMT system effectively addresses the name translation problem by considering names as a central part of the translation task from the start, rather than an afterthought. The system's ability to adapt to different name translation patterns and to prioritize high-value words according to importance gives it functional advantages beyond existing MT technologies. The proposed evaluation metric further ensures that such improvements can be objectively measured and tracked, providing a complete solution to enhance the capability of MT systems for conveying comprehensive and accurate information across languages. response: Certainly, here is my answer: Introduction Over many decades, social scientists have sought to formalize successful modes of interaction in social and communication situations. This includes the seminal work of H.P. Grice (1975), who famously developed a theory of cooperative communication behavior. A particular cornerstone of this theory is the cooperative principle, which questions how interlocutors interact so as to serve the evolving goals of a conversation. This principle yields "maxims" - conventions and strategies (such as 'be relevant', be truthful', 'use few words', and 'avoid ambiguity') that speakers commonly strive to adhere to, at least when societal norms and knowledge constraints allow it. At first glance, the application of such maxims seem rooted in social reasoning, often framed as a domain-specific theory connected to moral instinct, social norms, or derived directly from inference among semantic meanings. However, in recent years, there has been a growing interest in the idea that cooperative communication could be understood and even explained through more general, domainindependent theories. This paper contributes to this line of inquiry, by examining how Gricean maxims might emerge from rational multi-agent decision-making processes. The core of multi-agent decision theory centers around questions of what oracles rational actors intuitively rely upon to guide their choices, especially in view of the actions and knowledge of their peers. These questions are often framed within models specifically designed for this purpose, the most prevalent among them being the Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (Dec-POMDP). This class of models stems from Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) (e.g., Bellman, 1957) but extends them by considering agents in partially observable environments, where each agent is uncertain of the outcome of its own actions and those of other agents, and also uncertain of the initial states and real values of decision variables. The 'decentralized' aspect means agents are not assumed to have direct access to global, common knowledge or coordinated planning; rather, they must reason independently about the potential beliefs and preferences of others. Pomdp models are often associated with idealized rationality — assuming agents can reason perfectly or optimally within these complex frameworks. However, for confronting real-world scenarios, simplifications or heuristics are often necessary. Accommodating such cognitively motivated deviations allows us to better align theoretical models with human behavior. Consequently, our approach in this paper deviates from the ideal of perfect rationality and favors heuristic decision-making mechanisms inspired by human cognition. Our hypothesis is that when such an approach is applied within a multi-agent decision-making scenario, the emergent behavior will almost unintentionally resemble the Gricean maxims. This hypothesis rests on two complementary notions: (i) that rational but cognitively limited agents will develop strategies for efficient communication — both to convey necessary information and to account for the varying competencies and expectations within the group; and (ii) this process will naturally lead to a set of emergent conventions (or 'maxims') that approximate the cooperative principle, as these strategies prove empirically useful in maximizing joint utility across repeated interactions. To test this idea, we design an experimental framework centered around a simplified cooperative language task, where agents must communicate effectively to achieve a shared goal. The Dec-POMDP model structure includes both functional successful communication (reaching the goal) and the development of strategy as complexity increases (the type of communication that is observed). We compare our findings with baseline models that either do not reason about others' beliefs or do not employ heuristics, highlighting where our model produces strategies and communication conventions that align with Grice's maxims. Our methodology integrates two key advances.

While well-established methods exist for coreference resolution when labeled data are available (Hendrickx et al., 2009;Ponzetto and Navigli, 2008), the task of unsupervised coreference resolution is more challenging. The lack of labeled data requires techniques that can learn to identify coreference relationships based on the text alone. The extracted coreference chains have been shown to be useful for various NLP tasks including question answering, summarization, and machine translation (Riezler et al., 2007;Hemphill et al., 2009;Casanueva et al., 2011). In this paper, we approach the problem of unsupervised coreference resolution by discovering the most informative relations between mentions. Instead of relying on the surface-level features or similarity between mentions as in many existing approaches (Raghunathan et al., 2009;Huang and Rambow, 2013), our method focuses on identifying the relations between mention pairs that carry the most information about whether they should be coreferenced or not. Our approach learns different relation types between mentions and assigns an informativeness score to each relation based on how accurately it distinguishes coreferent from non-coreferent mention pairs. We show that the coreference chains predicted by our method outperform those produced by existing unsupervised methods on all benchmark data sets, significantly improving the accuracy of unsupervised coreference resolution. Assuming that coreference relationships are not always represented by a single, generic relation and that different types of relationships between mentions carry different amounts of information about their coreference status, we hypothesize that the most informative relations can be used effectively for unsupervised coreference resolution if one can identify and score the different relation types between mention pairs accurately. They are the most challenging to recover due to their inherently unbounded nature, making them prone to long-distance dependencies and violates maximum span assumptions that are common in many parsing algorithms (Jing et al., 2013). This has led to them being ignored in many areas of NLP, including parser evaluations. However, the significance of UD's can not be understated. They are found in nearly every aspect of natural language, ranging from comparatives and superlatives, to cleft constructions and complex predicate structures (Huddleston, 1994;Borsley, 2003). Moreover, despite their relative infrequency in corpora, they highlight the limitations of existing parser technologies. This paper presents a novel aspect of dependency grammar, by detailing the challenges presented by unbounded dependencies and evaluating the performance of state-of-the-art parsers on a newly created corpus of 700 sentences carefully annotated with UD's spanning seven different grammatical constructions. The traditional focus of parser evaluations has been on general-purpose dependency parser performance for achieving Parseval scores, which measure the total number of dependencies correctly identified relative to a given gold standard. However, this metric only provides a limited perspective on parser capabilities. It fails to recognize the complex nature of natural language while also neglecting the need for detailed analysis of parser weaknesses. This oversight has several implications. Firstly, it can lead to the erroneous impression that high Parseval scores indicate a parser's ability to tackle all linguistic phenomena, especially those involving complex dependency structure. Secondly, it can prevent the development of more sophisticated parsing techniques targeting specific grammatical constructs, such as UD's, which are crucial for NLP applications requiring deep understanding of language (e.g., question answering, text analysis, machine translation). The fundamental issue lies in the excessive reliance on Parseval scores as a yardstick for parsing quality. Parseval scores only account for the total number of dependencies a parser can correctly identify. However, this metric does little to differentiate between different types of dependencies or to explicitly penalize parsers for missing challenging linguistic structures, such as UD's. Furthermore, it places a uniform value on all dependencies, regardless of importance or grammatical complexity. This methodology risks overlooking anomalies or outlier sentences that challenge a parser’s ability in complex constructions. For example, a parser might achieve high Parseval scores by robustly recovering common dependencies while failing miserably with UD's, such as those found in comparative clauses or cleft constructions. This inherently challenges state-of-the-art parsers by exposing their performance limitations in recovering both common and less frequent but linguistically significant dependencies. The purpose here is not merely to emphasize the low recovery rates observed but to underscore the critical gap between current parser capabilities and the linguistic demands of natural language, especially in areas less frequent in evaluation corpora but still critical for language understanding. Our corpus, from which these results emerge, is constructed using annotated data that deliberately includes challenging unbounded dependencies, distinguishing it from traditional evaluation corpora that might avoid or overlook these constructions due to their infrequency. The seven grammatical constructions examined span various types of UD's, ensuring a comprehensive yet focused test of parsing technologies. These include but are not limited to relative clauses, comparative constructions, and clefts. The evaluation results show a wide range of performance among the parsers tested, with accuracy rates varying from 25% to 59%

response: Training natural language processing (NLP) algorithms reliably on mostly native data to improve non-native's writing poses two significant barriers. The first is that learners may use articles and prepositions in different ways, which cannot be captured by mostly native data. The second is that learners make errors that native speakers almost never make and, thus, are not captured in typical n-gram or pattern-based models trained on native corpora (Ehret and Ngai, 2010;Strube and Baldwin, 1995). In this paper, we present an approach to error correction in learner writing that tackles these two challenges simultaneously. Building on a representation of learner texts as a knowledge error graph, we optimize a meta-classifier to assemble evidence from four distinct engines: a language model, and three error-specific classifiers trained from large mostly native resources. The core of language models is n-gram which represents the probability of a word appearing at a position, given the previous (n−1) words. The indispensable training data for n-gram models are, however, very sizeable corpora. For example, one may need 100 million sentences and a total of about one trillion word tokens to train a 5-gram model with high accuracy. Such volumes of data are impractical for applications such as information retrieval or data extracted from online social network due to the limited space and time constraints (e.g., we usually want to process a few queries per second while serving many users at the same time). As a result, training big language models is very challenging, and online algorithms have recently been proposed to adapt the language models online in the places of big language models pre-trained from large corpora (Chen and Manning, 2014;Zoph and Le, 2016). In these cases, the handling of very large amounts of n-gram information and the efficiency of these models are very crucial. As proposed by Kaplan and Finkel (2002), a suffix tree can be used to efficiently represent this context information. The suffix tree provided a way to represent n-gram data in the sense that each n-gram becomes a node while the path representing the word sequence is the n-gram itself. However, several points must also be addressed when using suffix trees for n-gram language models. First, suffix trees naturally have higher memory requirements than linear representations as in, for example, the classic suffix array in (Gao et al., 2011) because a tree has pointers and storage for each node needed to represent the n-gram and their contexts (e.g., the previous n−1 words) which would grow exponentially with the vocabulary size. Traditional feature weighting schemes, such as TF-IDF, are inadequate here because they weigh terms proportionally to their frequency, without considering their potential structural significance – i.e., how much they help to organize the content and convey the meaning of a text. In this paper, we propose a novel Rhetorical Structure Index (RSI) that aims to quantify the structural importance of a word or a phrase. Unlike content-driven measurements, RSI considers structural information in its formulation. We demonstrate the applicability of RSI on the task of segmenting unstructured lecture transcripts into meaningful segments. The results show that using RSI significantly improves the segmentation accuracy compared to TF-IDF, a traditional content-based feature weighting scheme. Unstructured Text and Its Structure Structural cues in text are usually studied in the context of Rhetorical Structure Theory (RST) (Mann and Thompson, 1988). While discourse in English (as well as in similar languages) is often structured in a top-down fashion, for example, with main clauses at the top, followed by subordinate clauses that provide additional information about the main clause, this structure is not encoded in syntax alone. RST is a theory that tries to specifically capture these assumed relationships while the syntax attempts to capture syntactic relationships in a more formal and bottom-up way. One core concept in RST is that of connectives or discourse markers: words like "however," "therefore," "meanwhile," and "additionally" which can indicate relationships between different parts of a text, signaling, for instance, a contrast or an addition. However, not all structurally significant words are marked by such overt discourse markers. A potential "minimal unit of meaning" or "meaning unit" in RST could be considered as one structured discourse unit, which could be less or more than a sentence. However, identifying a single word, phrase, or a contiguous segment as a "structural cue" is another matter. Our RSI aims to fill this gap by providing a computational framework and metric to identify such elements. response: Certainly, here is my answer: Introduction Computational argumentation mining (AM) is an emerging field that aims at automatically analyzing and understanding argumentative structures from natural language discourse. It has numerous applications in various domains, including legal, medical, and social sciences, as well as online forums and social media. Current research efforts in AM emphasize on questions such as "What is the argument involved and who supports it?" and "What are the claims, premises, and links that form the argument?" (Hirohisa et al., 2019;Mihalcea and Wacholder, 2015;Lippi and Tannese, 2016). Traditional approaches in AM rely heavily on handcrafted rules, domain-specific knowledge, and syntactic patterns (Arasasingham et al., 2011;Docherty et al., 2010;Mihalcea and Wiebe, 2007;Mani and Maybury, 2008). While these techniques are sometimes effective, they are often rigid, fragile, and require considerable domain-specific effort to maintain. As a result, there is growing interest in achieving end-to-end, data-driven approaches that learn to perform AM tasks directly from raw text. The advent and success of deep learning techniques have facilitated significant progress in natural language processing (NLP), specifically in sequence labeling, dependency parsing, and other related tasks. These techniques hold the potential to revolutionize AM by leveraging neural architectures that can learn complex patterns and structures from data without relying on explicit syntactic or semantic features (Vinyals et al., 2015;Chen and Manning, 2014;Graff and Kong, 2019;Zhou and Xu, 2015). However, real-world AM datasets are often limited in scale, heterogeneous in input styles, and lack gold-standard annotations, which makes applying standard neural techniques or transfer learning from English or other high-resource languages challenging. Our investigation aims to explore a novel end-to-end learning framework for AM. Instead of breaking down the task into component parts or abstracting away linguistic complexity, we opt for a less-segmented and more integrated approach that seeks to model argument structures directly from byte-pair encoded (BPE) token sequences or tokenized sentences. We frame AM as two distinct but interrelated tasks: (1) token-based dependency parsing, where dependencies structure the argument as a graph of atoms, and (2) token-based sequence tagging (labeling the types of arguments and their structural roles). Both tasks are considered in a multi-task framework to leverage shared and complementary information. The novelty and potential benefit of our approach lie in its end-to-end nature, elegantly sidestepping the trade-offs and complexities associated with traditional hand-engineered patterns or hierarchical decomposition. At the same time, the multi-task setup offers the possibility to hone and cross-validate the model's understanding of AM-specific nuances, even without specific annotations for hierarchical structures like argument components. We experiment with a range of neural architectures, including bidirectional LSTM (BiLSTM), transformers, and graph neural networks (GNNs), to see which best capture the AM patterns. Our approach is also highly functional in that it could easily extend to other languages and domains, given the right training data, a flexibility not as easily achieved with rule-based systems. However, framing AM as a comprehensive dependency parsing task, akin to common NLP tasks like English sentence parsing, reveals a particular challenge. The complexity and variability of argument structures often defy the rules and patterns traditionally used for dependency parsing

Specifically, they cause recognition failures and can lead to error propagation through the pipeline, negatively impacting the performance of downstream applications, such as spoken language understanding and spoken document retrieval. Recognizing OOV regions accurately is even more critical in specialized domains, where the lexicon can be limited or dynamic. At present, the detection of OOV regions in speech is typically addressed as a binary classification task, where features are extracted locally from each potential OOV region and a classifier (e.g., a Support Vector Machine (SVM), decision trees, or recurrent neural network (RNN)) is trained on these local features to classify the region as OOV or known vocabulary (V). However, this local, modular approach fails to leverage the rich context available in speech. For example, SVMs (and other popular classifiers) for OOV detection typically use local acoustic or language-model based features extracted over a small context window (e.g., 3-5 seconds) surrounding each potential OOV word (Kim and Banerjee, 2012). This locality makes it difficult to incorporate subtle cues that may indicate OOV words, such as inconsistency with surrounding words or speakers deviating from their typical pronunciation for OOV words, or the acoustic properties of OOV words themselves, especially if phonetically different from in-vocabulary words. Moreover, OOV detection benefits from a consideration of local context and "long-range dependence" in human speech, such as syntactic structure, semantic coherence, and idiomatic expressions that can provide additional contextual clues. AES systems today still largely rely on carefully designed features to evaluate and score essays. These features include features related to length, vocabulary, grammatical correctness, and more. However, the ideal set of features is not only difficult to design, but also may vary depending on questions or topics asked. In this paper, we explore an alternative to feature-based AES systems. Instead of designing features, we let the machine learn a useful representation of essays and their scores directly from the word sequence itself. We use a neural network model that learns how to predict the score of an essay given its text, without any feature engineering beforehand, and report on its performance. Previous research on AES often viewed the problem as one of extracting features from essays in order to then use these features as input to a dedicated score prediction model. The feature extraction process places constraints on the final system - for example, how well it might generalize to essays of different lengths, or to essays on new topics. For instance, looking for keywords in the essay may work well in a system designed to score essays that are about specific scientific topics, but this approach may not generalize well to essays that ask students to discuss or argue on broad topics like ethics, arts, or politics. A model that learns feature representations directly from essays may be better able to capture the shallow structures and deeper semantic features that are useful for general-purpose AES. In this work, we focus on a type of neural network architecture known as a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN), specifically a variant called a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network, due to its demonstrated ability to handle sequential data such as text. An LSTM is capable of learning to focus on different parts of the essay while keeping track of what has been read before, which is necessary for capturing the context and meaning of an essay. We explore several architectures, including simple RNNs, and more complex ones like LSTMs or LSTM-based encoder-decoder models. The encoder-decoder architecture, for instance, is often used for machine translation tasks but can also be used for sequence generation tasks. For AES, we can think of scoring as generating a continuous prediction for each essay, which is exactly the kind of task an encoder-decoder model might be suitable for. Our primary evaluation metric is the quadratic weighted Kappa (QWK), a multi-choice accuracy measure widely used in AES, as it gives a more robust measure than simple zero-one accuracy because real world scores such as 9/10 are not always uniform. We used a public dataset of essays and their scores provided by the Automated Student Assessment Prize (ASAP), a competition organized by The CommonLit and The William and Flora Hewlett Foundation. This dataset allows us to evaluate the performance of our models across a wide range of essays on a variety of topics, written by students with different skill sets and backgrounds. Our primary finding is that the best-performing model, a multi-layer LSTM network, outperforms a strong baseline system by 5.6% in terms of QWK. Temporal information extraction (TimeX) is one of the key tasks that can significantly improve the performance of question answering systems (QA). TimeX, as defined by (Tanev et al., 2002), is the task of automatically extracting verbs or event time expressions and identifying temporal constraints among events, i.e., identifying temporal relationships. TimeX is a crucial task for various applications, such as answering temporal questions, event alignment, temporal knowledge graph construction, summarization, and more. The problem of extracting temporal information can be viewed as a part of the "Relation Extraction" problem that has been actively studied in the NLP community (e.g., the Semeval 2010 and Semeval2013 tasks) (Barzilay and Lapata, 2008; Hendrickx et al., 2009). Different approaches have been proposed for this task, including hand-engineered features, machine learning, and deep learning methods (e.g., the works focusing on extraction of temporal relations assumed in the FrameNet corpus (Lin and Pantel, 2001)). However, to the best of our knowledge, no work has been proposed for analyzing temporal information (e.g., whether the event is past, present, or future) using word embeddings or representations in an end-to-end learning framework based on sequential models. From the viewpoint of NLP, TimeX is related to a broad range of tasks, such as temporal reasoning, temporal ordering, and frame semantic analysis (Allen, 1984). Temporal understanding is also central to natural language understanding (e.g., question answering and text summarization; Krapivsky et al., 2005; Pan et al., 2015). For instance, when answering temporal questions like "At what time did event X happen?", knowledge about event time is a necessary piece of information. Similarly, when answering forecasting questions like "What will happen after event X?", knowledge about the temporal ordering of events is necessary. In recent years, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997) have been applied successfully to various NLP tasks. LSTM-based models are particularly well-suited for sequence-based tasks such as language modeling (Mikolov et al., 2010; Le and Mikolov, 2014) and machine translation (Sutskever et al., 2014). However, the application of LSTMs to TimeX is novel and presents some unique challenges. In this paper, we propose a comprehensive approach to time extraction using LSTM-based models. Our architecture leverages syntactic dependencies as a primary source of information across different levels of granularity (intra-sentence, cross-sentence, document-level). We exploit the shortest functional dependency paths between entities to obtain a simple representation of temporal relationships. To enhance the model's performance, we have introduced a novel "double-checking" approach that increases recall for positive cases without significantly impacting precision. This allows us to capture more rare but positive temporal relationships. Additionally, a global conflict resolution technique is employed to handle contradictory, dynamic, or contextually dependent relations.

response: Certainly, here is my answer: Introduction Event schema induction (ESI) is an important problem in natural language processing (NLP). Knowledge of event schemas is crucial for various applications, including information extraction, event detection and event ordering (Eisenstein and O'Connor, 2015;Narayanan, 2013; questions answering (Lin et al., 2014), and narrative understanding (Mao et al., 2016). An event schema consists of a set of slots and their possible fillers (e.g., for “Professor wins award”, an event schema can include “Professor” as the person, “wins” as the action, and “award” as the object). Inducing event schemas is challenging due to the following reasons: (i) limited amount of labeled data to directly model relationships among semantic entities (i.e., entities related by event); (ii) entities making up an event can be complex (e.g., containing modifiers such as "an armed man"); and (iii) a given entity can participate in multiple event types (e.g., "a man" can be associated with various events such as "a man sits", "a man eats", "a man runs"). Early work in ESI primarily focuses on identifying event Schemas and their roles from small domains (e.g., news articles). These early studies assumed fixed event schemas and assumed that the roles of entities in these events are straightforward (e.g., head entities and their associations to the core event verbs). More recent work deviates from this assumption and aims to discover event Schemas and roles (slots) as well, using various approaches (Ahrari and Kim, 2010;Singh and Anand, 2014;Huang et al., 2014;Rashkin and Chaturvedi, 2016). However, while these studies do not specify assumptions about the number or types of event Schemas or their roles, most methods in the literature assume that the entities involved in the event are primarily represented as head terms (like "man", "eat", or "vaccine candidate"), possibly with a simple and fixed set of modifiers (e.g., changing the head to "an armed man"). It might be valuable to also use additional information provided by more complex elements such as pre-modifiers (e.g., "armed man"), post-modifiers, or determiners (e.g., "the award"). For example, the modifier "armed" can show that the role of "man" is possibly related more to an action of threat or violence in the event of "an armed man attacks", rather than a general role of "a man". Language models, such as generative models, are typically used to generate compositional representations of text. But these models typically sum independent information from entities (modelling disjoint probabilities), while they should consider joint probabilities of any extended combinations of entities that are interesting or meaningful, like "armed man" as a comprehensive type of "man". Our work addresses this gap by proposing a generative model for event schema induction that incorporates the syntax and semantics provided by head words and their modifiers. Our work proposes a novel goal-directed random walk (GD-RW) algorithm that aims to increase the efficiency and accuracy of random walks. The core idea of GD-RW is to set a specific inference target at each step so that this target can direct and guide random walks towards structures that are more likely beneficial for inferring the target. While they appear to be less complex than verbs or nouns, they exhibit a rich and varied behavioral profile. A preposition may carry different meanings depending on context. A particular preposition may show different tendencies depending on its complement phrase, scope status, or attachment to modal or aspectual verbs. This range and nuance of prepositional behavior, while somewhat expected based on current theory, has actually confounded the development of appropriate word-embedding and lexicon-enhanced systems for even very basic language tasks due to a lack of understanding of these subtleties. At the same time, there is a dearth of vocabulary resources for prepositions. While dictionaries are very well established for verbs and nouns, the typical online or traditional English-language dictionary entry for a preposition reflects the historical but outdated practice of glossing the "core" usage(s) without reflecting the full range of senses and behaviors of prepositions in various contexts. This core usage may not be representative of the creative and productive ways in which English speakers use prepositions in diverse sentences and discourse. For instance, the core use of between may emphasize referential objects (We are running between the buildings) while a figurative use may refer to abstract or temporal points (The new policy is between different ideological stances or Stay between 6 and 8 pm). This paper presents the Pattern Dictionary of English Prepositions (PDEP), a new lexical resource for the study of preposition behavior. This dictionary is distinct from existing linguistic resources in focusing on the patterns of prepositional usage across diverse contexts. Instead of limiting the study to "standard" or core usage (as is the case with a traditional dictionary), PDEP provides a reference point for analysis of preposition behaviors across a wide range of contextual and syntactic features. Understanding the contextual nuances and patterns of preposition usage is critical for several areas of natural language processing (NLP), including: - More accurate part-of-speech tagging and parsing. - Enhanced sense disambiguation and semantic role labeling. - Improvements in machine translation or cross-lingual NLP projects confronting similar challenges across languages. - More effective adaptation of prepositions in paraphrasing, summarization, or other NLP tasks that rely on understanding of nuanced meaning. response: Training natural language parsers typically involves large-scale annotated corpora. However, while recent advances have led to efficient unsupervised and weakly supervised approaches, supervision remains the most common method for high-performance deep parsers (Krishnamurthy and Kollar, 2013). Specifying the particular forms of the grammatical, semantic, and discourse annotations is questionspecific, but collecting and processing these annotations is often labor-intensive and costly. A recent alternative to traditional human annotation practices is crowdsourcing, where large tasks can be split into many smaller parts that are completed by many inexpensive workers. However, this comes with its own set of challenges, particularly how to ensure task quality while minimizing training time, cost, and effort. Crowdsourcing offers an alternative for tasks that are difficult to accomplish by fully-automated methods or inhouse annotation. It has been successful in a wide range of semantic parsing tasks including part-of-speech tagging, named entity recognition, and semantic role labeling (Derczynski and Ngonga Ngomo, 2013). However, discourse analysis, as a challenging, creative and thus timeconsuming task, has been less studied in the context of crowdsourcing. As proposed by Kaplan and Maxwell (1988), or as studied recently by Crouch et al. (2014) or Cossock et al. (2014), shallow discourse structures are typically defined through discourse relations. However, discourse structure can also be represented more deeply at the discourse level, revealing complex, long-range patterns of coherence such as anaphora or dialog structure (e.g., Grosz and Sidner, 1986;Baker et al., 1998;Das and Smith, 1993). We focus on this latter and harder-to-automate analysis approach: annotating discourse structure that is global in nature and is inconsistent across sentences. For this, detailed and accurate discourse annotations are required. This means crowdannotated discourse can only result from careful crowdsourcing design of tasks, guidelines and interfaces, a focus we take as the contribution of this work. The contribution of our work is twofold. First, we present a task design that successfully splits a complex discourse structure annotation into two feasible sub-tasks, and hence can be performed by untrained workers. Resultantly, we are able to annotate a large number of sentences in a short time. Second, we apply these annotations to train a supervised discourse structure parser and evaluate its results. Therefore, our work also contributes a real-world corpus of 30,000 Japanese sentences with discourse annotations. These annotations are based on an annotation framework proposed in the previous work (Noto et al., 2017) and designed with the consideration of the tutorial by Deecke and Schwall (2003). The idea of using simplified guidelines for general discourse annotation has been realized by crowdsourcing tools such as BRAT (Stenetorp et al., 2012) or autoEdit (de Marneffe and Manning, 2008). However, users tend to struggle with the complexity of discourse annotation and are likely to give up unless the task is simplified. Our task design was based on separating harder and easier sub-tasks, as Grosof et al. (2010) suggested. Our task design enables untrained non-experts to perform the annotation without much background knowledge, thereby achieving fast annotation of the entire corpus. A task designer might expect to realize some quality compromise for this advantage, but our results will verify whether the loss is least when trained models are restricted to the simplified annotations presented here. response: Certainly, here is my answer: Introduction Over the past few years, there has been a significant increase in the availability of unlabeled text data. To extract information from this vast unstructured data, information extraction (IE) techniques have gained prominence. There are several forms of IE tasks including but not limited to named entity recognition (NER) and relation extraction. Named entity recognition refers to the process of identifying and systematically categorizing words, phrases, or idioms which are part of the pre-defined list (person, organization, location, etc.). Entity relation extraction (ER) is a more complex task that involves identifying and establishing relationships between entities. These techniques are essential for knowledge base construction, text summarization, question answering systems, and natural language understanding tasks in general. Each of these tasks can be approached using supervised learning methods. However, just like in other supervised learning tasks, semantic features (i.e., context, meaning, or relation) are essential for accurate modeling, and these features are difficult to capture manually. Traditional approaches often rely on various handcrafted features such as looking for keywords, NER-tagged output, or syntactic parsing output, which often require extensive manual effort. As a result, these tasks are frequently treated as sequential or independent, which might or might not capture the full interaction and correlation between this context, meaning and relation symbols. In this work, we propose to jointly model the extractions of entities and relations using the Minimum Risk Training (MRT) framework. The MRT framework has been used effectively to address coreference resolution tasks by exploring the extent to which different entity mentions are likely to be associated (Sang and Ng, 2005;Sang and Ng, 2007). Here, we extend this approach to also handle the extraction of entity relationships and their respective entities. The joint approach is rationalized under the belief that it is beneficial to learn the interaction between entities and relations simultaneously, rather than treating them as separate and independent tasks. The proposed model can significantly improve performance over independent methods by leveraging the interaction between the two tasks. Our model also demonstrates the advantage of a lightweight learning architecture since our implementation is simple yet effective. Our method outputs rich relational data which can be utilized in several downstream NLP/NLU tasks such as question answering, natural language inference, and information retrieval systems. In this paper, we first discuss the formulation of the joint entity and relation extraction problem. We then describe our MRT-based approach. Next, we present our experimental results which demonstrate the effectiveness of our joint model on the widely used ACE 2005 and NYT datasets.
